item.title: Best Productivity Apps for Developers and Indie Hackers in 2026
item.description: Five task tools for solo developers running AI coding agents in 2026 — what each one does with MCP, and where each one stops.
item.content:encoded:
On this page

  • The core problem: context-switching kills agent workflows
  • Dovilo: built for the agent-aware developer
  • Linear: project tracking with an MCP server
  • Notion: flexible but not agent-native
  • Todoist: reliable task management, no agent awareness
  • Obsidian with Tasks plugin: local-first, fully custom
  • A note on focus tools
  • How to choose
  • Get started with Dovilo
  • Frequently asked questions

By Selahaddin Akgün

If you're a solo developer or indie hacker running AI coding agents in 2026, the best productivity apps aren't the ones with the most features. They're the ones that don't break your flow.

The real problem isn't finding a to-do list. It's that your task list and your coding agent live in completely separate worlds — and every time you switch between them, you lose the thread. The agent finishes something. You go update the task. You come back. Ten minutes gone, and your mental model of where you were has quietly evaporated.

Most productivity apps were built before AI agents became a daily workflow tool. They're fine at storing tasks. They have no idea what Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, or Gemini CLI is doing right now, what it just finished, or what it should pick up next. That gap costs real time and attention.

This list focuses on tools that actually serve the solo dev and indie hacker workflow in 2026, with honest notes on where each one fits and where it doesn't.

The core problem: context-switching kills agent workflows

When you're running an AI coding agent, two things need to stay in sync: what the agent is working on, and what you're tracking as a human. Most setups today look like this — a markdown file or a Notion doc with tasks, a terminal running an agent, and a lot of manual copy-pasting between them.

The tools below each solve a different piece of this. None of them solve everything. Pick based on your actual workflow.

Dovilo: built for the agent-aware developer

Dovilo is the only tool on this list designed specifically around the idea that your coding agent should work from a task queue it can read and update — without touching your personal to-do list.

Here's how it works in practice. The desktop app (Windows and macOS, part of Pro) runs a local MCP server over stdio. Your agent — whether that's Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, or any MCP client configured via JSON — connects to it and gets 9 tools: 3 read, 6 write. It can read tasks, update status, and log progress. It cannot create tasks or delete them. That constraint is intentional. You stay in control of what goes into the queue.

The agent works from a separate AI task queue scoped to a project. Your personal task list — called My Tasks — is not on the MCP tool surface at all. It never appears. So you can track your own notes, ideas, and personal work without any risk of the agent touching them.

MCP traffic stays local. There's no Dovilo internet endpoint involved. The only external calls are the ones your agent makes to its own model provider. That matters if you're working on anything sensitive, or if you'd simply rather not have your task data routing through a third-party cloud.

On the webhook side (documented at dovilo.app/docs/webhooks), Dovilo fires task.created and task.status_changed events, signed with HMAC-SHA256 and retried up to 5 times. That's enough to wire up Slack notifications, Linear updates, or an n8n automation without writing a polling loop.

The focus side of the app is a full Pomodoro timer — 25-minute work, 5-minute break — with six ambient scenes, five of them in the Focus Ambience Pack. Finished tasks and completed focus sessions earn bricks, which go toward an isometric city you build on a grid. Nothing decays. If you have a quiet week, your city just waits. There's no streak to break, no guilt attached.

Tasks and focus sessions are free and unlimited on iOS and Android, with no ads on any tier. Pro is $2.49/month, $19.99/year, or $49.99 lifetime, with a 7-day trial started in the mobile app. Desktop is part of Pro.

What Dovilo doesn't do yet (as of September 2026): No data export. No remote MCP — the agent runs on the machine where Desktop is installed. Both are on the public roadmap.

Best for: Solo developers and indie hackers running AI coding agents who want the agent working from a real task queue — not a markdown file — with a clear boundary between agent work and personal tasks.

Linear: project tracking with an MCP server

Linear is a project management tool built for software teams, though plenty of solo devs use it. It has a clean keyboard-driven UI, solid GitHub integration, and its own MCP server. Since June 2026 it also executes work: assign an issue to Linear Agent and a coding session runs Claude Code or Codex in a cloud sandbox, then hands back a diff for review.

It's genuinely good at tracking bugs, features, and milestones. Where it's less suited for solo indie hackers is the overhead — concepts like cycles, teams, and triage queues add friction when you're one person. The free tier covers the basics; Basic is $10 per user per month and Business $16, both billed annually (as of September 2026, per Linear's pricing page).

Best for: Developers already using Linear for project management who want agent access to their issue tracker.

Notion: flexible but not agent-native

Notion is the most flexible tool on this list. You can build any task system you want inside it, and it ships an MCP server so agents can read and write to your workspace.

The flexibility is also the friction. You have to build your own task structure from scratch. There's no Pomodoro timer, no focus mode, no ambient sound. And because the agent can access your whole workspace depending on how you configure permissions, the boundary between "agent work" and "my notes" is something you have to manage yourself.

Notion's free tier is generous. Paid plans start at $12/user/month (as of September 2026, per Notion's pricing page).

Best for: Developers who already live in Notion and want to keep everything in one place, and are comfortable managing agent permissions themselves.

Todoist: reliable task management, no agent awareness

Todoist is one of the most polished task managers available — natural language input, recurring tasks, priority levels, clean mobile experience. It's been around long enough to be genuinely reliable.

Doist ships an official MCP server — @doist/todoist-mcp, hosted at ai.todoist.net/mcp, with an official Claude Code plugin — so an agent can read and write Todoist out of the box. The difference is scope. It connects over OAuth to your whole account, so the agent sees every project and every personal task, and it can create and delete them. That is fine if your Todoist is already a work queue. It is a different proposition if your task list is also where the rest of your life lives.

Free tier covers the basics. Pro is $5/month (as of September 2026, per Todoist's pricing page).

Best for: Developers who want a polished, reliable task manager and are comfortable giving an agent access to the whole account.

Obsidian with Tasks plugin: local-first, fully custom

Obsidian is a local markdown editor with a strong plugin ecosystem. The Tasks plugin turns markdown checkboxes into a queryable task system with due dates, recurrence, and filtering — everything living on your file system.

There's no built-in MCP server, but the community has built MCP integrations for Obsidian. Setup requires more configuration than anything else on this list. If you're comfortable with that, the result is a fully local, fully customizable system with no subscription required.

Best for: Developers who want maximum control and are willing to wire things together themselves.

A note on focus tools

A few tools worth naming that focus specifically on the Pomodoro and deep work side rather than task management:

Forest is a focus timer where you grow a virtual tree during sessions. Well-designed, mobile-first feel. No task management, no agent integration.

Be Focused Pro (macOS/iOS) is a clean Pomodoro timer with session logging. Again, no agent integration.

If you want something that combines focus sessions with task management and agent awareness in one app, Dovilo is the only tool on this list that does all three.

How to choose

Tool Agent-aware MCP server Focus timer Free tier
Dovilo Yes (local MCP) Yes, local over stdio Yes, Pomodoro 25/5 Yes, unlimited tasks/focus
Linear Partial Yes No Yes (limited)
Notion Partial Yes No Yes
Todoist Yes Yes (official, hosted) No Yes
Obsidian + Tasks Custom Community plugin No Yes

The right tool depends on what's actually slowing you down. If context-switching between your agent and your task list is the bottleneck, that narrows the list quickly.

Get started with Dovilo

MCP setup is documented at dovilo.app/ai. There's also an open-source LangGraph demo showing a full agent loop at github.com/slhddn/dovilo-langgraph-demo.

Download for iOS: App Store Download for Android: Google Play Desktop (Pro, Windows): Dovilo-Setup.exe Desktop (Pro, macOS): Dovilo.dmg

Frequently asked questions

Does Dovilo's MCP server work with Claude Code and Cursor? Yes. The desktop app runs a local MCP server over stdio. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and any MCP client configured via JSON can connect to it. Desktop is part of Pro ($2.49/month or $49.99 lifetime).

Can the agent see my personal to-do list? No. My Tasks is not on the MCP tool surface at all. The agent only sees the AI task queue for the project it's assigned to. Your personal tasks are invisible to it.

What can the agent actually do with Dovilo's MCP tools? It gets 9 tools: 3 read, 6 write. It can read tasks, update their status, and log progress. It cannot create tasks or delete them. You control what goes into the queue.

Does MCP traffic go through Dovilo's servers? No. The MCP server runs locally inside the desktop app over stdio. There is no Dovilo internet endpoint for MCP. The only external calls are the ones your agent makes to its own model provider.

Is there a free tier? Yes. Tasks and focus sessions (including Pomodoro) are free and unlimited on iOS and Android, with no ads on any tier. Desktop, MCP, webhooks, and cloud sync require Pro.

Does Dovilo support webhook integrations for Slack or Linear? Yes. Dovilo fires task.created and task.status_changed webhooks, signed with HMAC-SHA256, with up to 5 retries. Documentation is at dovilo.app/docs/webhooks.

Is remote MCP supported? Not yet (as of September 2026). The agent runs on the machine where Desktop is installed. Remote MCP is on the public roadmap.

item.title: Forest App Alternative: 5 Focus Apps With More Features
item.description: Looking for a Forest app alternative with real task management and gamification? These 5 focus apps go further than a simple timer.
item.content:encoded:
On this page

  • What Forest does well (and where it stops)
  • 5 Forest app alternatives with more features
    • 1. Dovilo — task manager, focus timer, and isometric city builder
    • 2. Habitica — RPG task manager with social accountability
    • 3. BeeDone — AI coaching with task management
    • 4. MainQuest — RPG progression with a focus timer
    • 5. Do It Now — RPG stats for daily habits
  • How these alternatives compare at a glance
  • Which alternative is right for you?
  • Frequently asked questions

Forest is a genuinely good app. The core mechanic — grow a virtual tree during a focus session, kill it if you leave the app — is simple and it works. But if you've been using it for a while, you've probably noticed the ceiling: no task list, no way to plan your day, no Pomodoro timer, no real desktop app. You're essentially paying for a phone-locking mechanism with a nice visual attached.

If you're looking for a Forest alternative because you want more than a countdown timer, the five apps below are worth your time. Each one includes focus session mechanics, but each adds something Forest doesn't — task management, gamification, ambient audio, or AI agent integration. Pick based on what's actually missing from your current setup.

What Forest does well (and where it stops)

A lot of comparison articles overstate Forest's feature set, so it's worth being precise.

Forest does one thing: it runs a countdown timer and grows a tree if you don't leave the app. There's no built-in to-do list. You can label a session, but that's not task management — no repeating tasks, no due dates, no priorities, no My Day view. The focus timer is a single countdown with no Pomodoro cycles and no break scheduling. Ambient sound options are limited. There are browser extensions for Chrome and Firefox, but no full desktop app.

What Forest does have is a real-tree-planting partnership with Trees for the Future, a large loyal user base, and a visual that genuinely motivates some people to stay off their phone. If phone-locking is your primary need and nothing else matters, Forest is fine. If you want a system that helps you decide what to work on and helps you work on it, you need something else.

5 Forest app alternatives with more features

1. Dovilo — task manager, focus timer, and isometric city builder

Dovilo combines three things Forest either separates or ignores entirely: a full task manager, a Pomodoro-style focus timer, and a visual reward system that goes well beyond growing a tree.

The task management side covers due dates, priorities, stars, flags, repeating tasks, reminders, and multiple views — My Day, Important, Planned, Flagged, and custom lists. That's comparable to a dedicated task manager, not a focus app with a notes field bolted on.

The focus timer runs as a single session, a Pomodoro cycle (25 minutes work, 5-minute break), or a session tied to a specific task. Do Not Disturb and background timer are both supported. Finish a session or complete a task and you earn bricks. Those bricks go into the Build market, where you spend them to construct and arrange an isometric city on a personal grid. Buildings don't decay. Your city grows as long as you keep working.

The ambient audio system is more developed than anything else in this category. There are six full-screen scenes — a default scene plus Rainy City, Midnight, Dusk, Snow, and Fog (those five come in the Focus Ambience Pack). A 12-layer sound mixer lets you blend up to three sounds at once. If you've had Forest's single rain loop on repeat and wished you could mix in a coffee shop or some distant thunder, this is the direct answer.

For developers specifically: Dovilo Desktop (Windows and macOS, included with Pro) runs a local MCP server. AI coding agents — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, or any MCP-compatible client via JSON — can connect to this server, read tasks from a dedicated AI task queue, execute them step by step, and report progress back to you. The agent works from a separate AI task queue; your personal to-do list is invisible to it. The server ships inside the Desktop app over stdio, so only the agent's own model calls leave your machine. The desktop app also supports signed webhooks to Slack, Linear, and n8n; documentation is at dovilo.app/docs/webhooks.

What Dovilo doesn't do yet: No data export. The MCP server is local only — it runs where Desktop runs, so there's no remote agent access. Desktop requires Pro. No social accountability features like group quests or shared progress.

Pricing: Free on iOS and Android, with tasks and Pomodoro sessions unlimited on the free tier. No ads on any tier. Pro is $2.49/month, $19.99/year (about $1.67/month, saving 33% versus monthly), or $49.99 as a one-time lifetime purchase. A 7-day free trial is available in the mobile app. The Focus Ambience Pack and Full City Package are each $4.99 as separate one-time purchases. AI task bundles start at $0.99 and never expire.

Best for: Anyone who wants Forest's visual motivation but also needs a real task manager. Developers using AI coding agents who want their task list and their agent working in the same loop.

Download on App Store or Google Play.

2. Habitica — RPG task manager with social accountability

Habitica takes a different approach to gamification: it turns your habits, dailies, and to-dos into an RPG character. Complete tasks and your character gains experience and gold. Skip them and your character takes damage. The social layer is Habitica's strongest differentiator — you can join parties, go on quests with friends, and face real consequences if someone in your group falls behind.

Task management depth is solid. Habits cover things you want to do repeatedly without a fixed schedule; dailies reset on a set cadence; to-dos are one-off items with optional due dates. There's reasonable flexibility in how you configure all three.

What Habitica doesn't have: a focus timer of any kind. No Pomodoro mode, no session tracking, no ambient audio. The visual style is retro pixel art, which some users love and others find immediately off-putting. As of September 2026, there's no AI agent integration and no desktop app beyond a browser interface.

Habitica has a large and genuinely active community. If social accountability is what keeps you on track and you don't need a focus timer, it's worth a look.

Best for: People motivated by social pressure and RPG progression who don't need a focus session mechanic.

3. BeeDone — AI coaching with task management

BeeDone is the most feature-complete task manager in this comparison after Dovilo. It includes task management with priorities and due dates, a focus timer, and an internal AI coaching layer that helps you decide what to work on and how to structure your day.

The AI in BeeDone is internal to the app — a coaching assistant, not an external agent interface. You can't connect Claude Code or Cursor to it. The reward visualization uses XP bars and badges rather than a spatial environment, which is more abstract than Forest's trees or Dovilo's city.

BeeDone doesn't publish pricing publicly, so you'll need to check their site directly to evaluate cost.

Best for: Users who want AI-assisted prioritization built into a task manager and don't need a visual city or agent integration.

4. MainQuest — RPG progression with a focus timer

MainQuest pairs RPG-style progression with a focus timer, which immediately puts it ahead of Forest in terms of feature breadth. You complete quests (tasks), run focus sessions, and advance your character through a fantasy progression system.

The task management side is lighter than Dovilo or BeeDone — the emphasis is on the RPG narrative layer rather than productivity infrastructure. There's no city-building mechanic. The focus timer works, but ambient audio options are limited. No AI agent integration as of September 2026.

Best for: Users who want an RPG story wrapped around their focus sessions and don't need deep task management.

5. Do It Now — RPG stats for daily habits

Do It Now maps your tasks and habits to RPG character stats. Complete tasks and your strength, intelligence, or charisma goes up depending on how you've categorized the work. It's a lighter gamification approach than Habitica's party system or Dovilo's city builder.

Focus timer functionality is present but basic — no Pomodoro configuration, no ambient audio, no AI integration. Task management covers the essentials (due dates, repeating tasks, priorities) without the depth of a dedicated task manager.

Best for: Users who want a simple stat-based RPG layer on top of habit tracking without a lot of complexity.

How these alternatives compare at a glance

App Task manager Focus timer Gamification style AI agent integration Free tier
Dovilo Full (due dates, repeats, priorities, My Day) Pomodoro + single + task-bound Isometric city builder Yes (MCP server, Pro + Desktop) Yes, unlimited tasks and focus
Habitica Full (habits, dailies, to-dos) None RPG character + social quests No Yes
BeeDone Full Yes XP bars + badges Internal AI only Check site
MainQuest Light Yes RPG quest progression No Check site
Do It Now Basic Basic RPG character stats No Yes
Forest None Single countdown only Tree growth No Limited

Which alternative is right for you?

You want a task manager and a focus timer together. Forest won't give you this. Dovilo, BeeDone, and Habitica (minus the timer) are the realistic options. Dovilo is the only one that includes all three — task management, Pomodoro timer, and visual reward — in a single free download.

You're motivated by social accountability. Habitica's party system is genuinely strong and has no equivalent in this list. If you need other people to keep you honest, Habitica is the right pick even without a focus timer.

You use AI coding agents daily. As of September 2026, Dovilo is the only app in this category with a local MCP server that external agents like Claude Code, Cursor, or Windsurf can connect to. If you're shipping code with an AI agent and want your task list in the same loop, that's a specific capability worth evaluating.

You just want a better focus timer with nicer audio. Dovilo's ambient sound system — six scenes, a 12-layer mixer, up to three sounds simultaneously — is more developed than anything else here. The free tier includes the default scene; the Focus Ambience Pack ($4.99 one-time) adds the remaining five.

You want the simplest possible upgrade from Forest. Do It Now or MainQuest add gamification without a steep learning curve. They're lighter apps for users who don't want to manage a full task system.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Forest alternative that also has a task manager? Yes. Dovilo includes a full task manager (due dates, priorities, repeating tasks, My Day view) alongside a Pomodoro focus timer and a visual city-building reward system. Habitica and BeeDone also include task management, though neither has Forest's visual focus mechanic.

Does Dovilo have a free version? Yes. Dovilo is free on iOS and Android with unlimited tasks and focus sessions, including Pomodoro, on the free tier. No ads on any tier. Pro adds advanced stats, ambient scenes, and desktop access at $2.49/month, $19.99/year, or $49.99 lifetime.

Which Forest alternative works on desktop? Dovilo Desktop runs on Windows and macOS and is part of Pro. It also runs a local MCP server for AI coding agent integration. Most other alternatives in this list are primarily mobile apps.

What does the MCP server in Dovilo actually do? It lets AI coding agents — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, or any MCP-compatible client — connect to a dedicated AI task queue in Dovilo, read tasks, execute them step by step, and report progress back. The agent works from a separate queue; your personal to-do list stays private. The server runs locally inside the Desktop app.

Does Dovilo have social features like Habitica's party quests? No. Dovilo has no group quests, shared accountability, or social features. If social pressure is what motivates you, Habitica is the better fit.

Can I use Dovilo offline? Yes. Tasks, focus sessions and city progress are stored on the device and work with no connection. Sync across devices is a Pro feature, and the desktop app itself requires Pro.

Is the Focus Ambience Pack worth buying separately? If ambient audio matters to your focus sessions, yes. The pack adds five full-screen scenes (Rainy City, Midnight, Dusk, Snow, Fog) and the 12-layer sound mixer for $4.99 as a one-time purchase. If you're already on the yearly or lifetime Pro plan and use the app daily, the per-session cost becomes negligible quickly.

Forest built a category. But the gap between what it offers and what a productive workday actually requires has grown. If you need a focus timer connected to a task list, something visual to show for your work, and — if you're a developer — a way to put your AI coding agent in the same loop, there are better options available today.

Dovilo is free to download on iOS and Android. Your city starts with the first task you finish.

item.title: TickTick Alternative: Which App Fits Your Workflow Better?
item.description: Find the right TickTick alternative for your workflow — from gamified task apps to AI-agent-ready tools for developers.
item.content:encoded:
On this page

  • Why people leave TickTick
  • Alternatives for general productivity and focus users
    • Todoist
    • Things 3
    • Forest
    • Habitica
    • MainQuest
  • Alternatives for developers running AI coding agents
    • Linear
    • Notion
  • Where Dovilo fits
    • Core task management
    • Pricing
    • What Dovilo doesn't do yet
  • Side-by-side comparison
  • Which alternative should you choose?
  • Frequently asked questions
  • The bottom line

If you're searching for a TickTick alternative, you probably already know what's bothering you. The app works fine — but something about the daily routine feels flat, or a specific gap keeps pulling you toward other tools. This article covers the most relevant alternatives across two distinct use cases: general productivity and focus users who want more motivation built into their workflow, and developers who want their task list to connect directly to an AI coding agent.

Which one describes you? Let's get into it.

Why people leave TickTick

TickTick is a capable, well-designed app. Tasks, calendars, Pomodoro timers, habit tracking — it covers a lot of ground in one interface. For most people, it's genuinely good.

The reasons people look elsewhere tend to fall into a few categories:

  • Motivation gap. Completing tasks feels like administration. There's no reward beyond a checkbox.
  • Price. TickTick Premium runs around $35.99/year. For solo users, that's worth weighing.
  • Developer workflow friction. TickTick has no official MCP server. There is an open API and community MCP servers, but nothing first-party built for coding agents. If you're running Cursor, Claude Code, or Windsurf, your task list and your agent live in completely separate worlds.
  • Focus-only needs. Some users want a timer with a light touch, not a full productivity suite.

None of these are complaints about quality. They're about fit. Here's how the main alternatives stack up.

Alternatives for general productivity and focus users

Todoist

Todoist is the most direct TickTick replacement for users who want a clean, reliable task manager. Natural language input, project organization, filters, and labels are all well-executed. The free tier is generous. Pro runs $5/month or $48/year.

What it doesn't offer: a built-in focus timer, any gamification, or anything that makes task completion feel like more than maintenance. If motivation is the problem, Todoist doesn't solve it.

Things 3

Things 3 is Apple-only and sold as a one-time purchase ($49.99 for Mac, $9.99 for iPhone). The design is excellent. The workflow — Areas, Projects, Today, Upcoming — suits people who think in terms of longer-horizon planning rather than daily urgency.

No Pomodoro timer, no gamification, no cross-platform support. If you're on Windows or Android, it's simply not an option.

Forest

Forest is a focus app, not a task manager. You plant a virtual tree when a session starts; it dies if you leave the app. That constraint works well for phone-free deep work.

There's no task list, no progression system beyond tree collection, and no full desktop app beyond browser extensions. If you need task management alongside focus, Forest covers only half the problem.

Habitica

Habitica turns your task list into an RPG. You create a character, complete tasks to earn experience and gold, and spend those rewards on gear and cosmetics. It has a large, active community.

The premium tier is $47.99/year and unlocks cosmetics only — not productivity features. There's no focus timer, no desktop app, and no AI agent integration. Habitica works well for users who respond to RPG mechanics and social accountability. It's less suited to solo developers or anyone who wants a persistent, spatial sense of progress rather than a character sheet.

MainQuest

MainQuest includes a built-in focus timer and uses character stats and loot as rewards for task completion. Several apps ship under this name with different pricing, so check the one you actually download before committing.

No desktop app, no spatial reward mechanic, no MCP integration. The reward loop is character-based rather than world-building-based, which suits some users and not others.

Alternatives for developers running AI coding agents

This is a narrower category, and the options are genuinely different.

Linear

Linear is the standard for AI-native task management in engineering teams. It's fast, well-designed, and deeply integrated with GitHub. Since June 2026 it also executes work: assign an issue to Linear Agent and a coding session runs Claude Code or Codex in a cloud sandbox, then returns a diff for review.

Linear costs $10 to $16 per user per month billed annually, and coding sessions consume separately purchased AI credits. Per-seat pricing, cycles and triage queues all assume a team. Nothing runs on your own machine either — the agent works in Linear's cloud against a repo it has been given access to. For a solo developer with a local checkout and a personal backlog, it's a team tool solving a different problem.

Notion

Notion can be configured as a task manager and supports MCP server connections. For developers already living in Notion who want to wire up an agent, it's a reasonable path. The tradeoff is that Notion is a general-purpose workspace, not a task-first app. Setup overhead is real, and the focus and motivation layers don't exist unless you build them yourself.

Where Dovilo fits

Dovilo sits at the intersection of both audiences above, which makes it unusual in this category.

On the productivity side, every completed task earns in-app currency called bricks. Those bricks go toward constructing and decorating a persistent isometric city. Buildings, streets, and structures accumulate over time as a direct reflection of your real-world output — a spatial, constructive reward loop rather than a character stat or a tree collection. Nothing decays.

On the developer tooling side, Dovilo Desktop runs a local MCP server. That server lets AI coding agents — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and any MCP-compatible client via JSON — read and update tasks from a dedicated AI task queue inside a project. The agent picks up work, executes it, and reports progress back without any manual copy-paste handoff between your task list and your coding tool. Your personal My Tasks list is not on the tool surface and is invisible to the agent; it sees only the AI task queue inside its assigned project.

Core task management

Dovilo covers due dates, priorities, stars, flags, repeats, and reminders. The unified view picker includes My Day, Important, Planned, and Flagged. Tasks and focus sessions — including Pomodoro 25/5 and task-bound timers — are free and unlimited on iOS and Android, with no ads on any tier.

Focus sessions run with background tracking and Do Not Disturb support. The ambience system includes six full-screen scenes and a 12-layer blendable sound mixer. Five of those scenes are in the standalone Focus Ambience Pack, available as a one-time purchase and included with Pro.

Pricing

The free tier covers tasks and focus with no limits and no ads. Pro Monthly is $2.49/month. Pro Yearly is $19.99/year ($1.67/month). Pro Lifetime is a one-time payment of $49.99. A 7-day free Pro trial is available in the mobile app — no charge if you cancel before it ends.

Desktop (Windows and macOS) is part of Pro. That means the MCP server, webhooks, and the desktop app itself all require a Pro plan. Webhooks support Slack, Linear, n8n, and custom services with signed delivery.

What Dovilo doesn't do yet

Worth being direct about the gaps:

  • No data export. There's currently no way to export your tasks or history to a file or another app.
  • No remote MCP. The MCP server runs locally inside Dovilo Desktop over stdio. The agent runs where Desktop runs. There's no hosted Dovilo endpoint.
  • Desktop requires Pro. The 7-day free trial starts in the mobile app; there's no desktop-only trial.

Both data export and remote MCP are on the public roadmap, but neither is available as of September 2026.

Side-by-side comparison

Feature TickTick Habitica Forest Dovilo
Task management Yes Yes No Yes
Focus timer Yes (Pomodoro) No Yes (only) Yes (Pomodoro + modes)
Gamification No RPG/avatar Tree collection City builder
Desktop app Yes No Browser only Yes (Pro)
MCP / AI agent integration No No No Yes (Pro, local)
Free tier Limited Yes Limited Yes (tasks + focus, no ads)
Price (annual) ~$35.99/yr $47.99/yr Varies $19.99/yr
Lifetime option No No No $49.99

Which alternative should you choose?

Choose Todoist if you want a clean, reliable task manager with no motivation layer and don't need focus timers or gamification.

Choose Things 3 if you're Apple-only and prefer a one-time purchase over a subscription.

Choose Forest if your only goal is phone-free focus sessions and task management isn't part of the picture.

Choose Habitica if RPG mechanics and social accountability are what keep you consistent.

Maybe you want a native desktop app, a built-in focus timer, or a reward system that feels more tangible than gold and gear. Whatever's driving the search, the gamified productivity space has grown considerably, and there are several strong options heading into 2026.

What Makes a Good Habitica Alternative?

Habitica's core loop is habit tracking and task management wrapped in an RPG combat system. You earn gold and experience by completing tasks, then spend it on gear and pets. The social layer — guilds, party quests — is a genuine draw for some users.

A good alternative should offer at least one meaningful improvement:

  • A built-in focus or Pomodoro timer

With that in mind, here are six apps worth considering.

1. Dovilo: Best for Developers and Focus-Driven Work

Dovilo is the most structurally different option on this list. Instead of an RPG combat loop, it runs on a city-building reward economy. Complete tasks and focus sessions, earn in-app currency called bricks, and spend those bricks for buildings, decorations, and upgrades that expand a personal isometric city.

The city is persistent. It doesn't reset when you miss a day or break a streak. Every building you place stays there, which makes progress feel genuinely cumulative rather than fragile.

Task Management

Dovilo's task manager supports due dates, priorities, stars, flags, and reminders. It's a full to-do system, not a stripped-down habit tracker. You can organize work the way you actually think about it — not just as a list of daily habits.

Focus Sessions

This is where Dovilo separates itself from every other app on this list. Three focus session modes are available: single session, Pomodoro cycle, and task-bound session. The Pro tier adds a Focus Ambience Pack with five full-screen ambient scenes and a 12-layer sound mixer that lets you blend up to three sounds at once. If you've ever wanted a Pomodoro timer paired with a proper ambient sound setup.

Developer-Specific Features

Dovilo Desktop ships a local MCP server that exposes a separate AI task queue — one per project, with a brief the agent reads first. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI connect to it and work from that queue. Your personal list is not on the tool surface at all: the agent cannot see it, and there is no create or delete tool, so it cannot add or remove tasks anywhere.

Signed webhooks also support Slack, Linear, and n8n, which makes it practical for solo founders who want their task system wired into the rest of their workflow.

Pricing

Dovilo is free to download. The Pro tier, which includes the desktop app and the Focus Ambience Pack, comes with a 7-day free trial. The Focus Ambience Pack is also available as a standalone one-time purchase. Pricing details are listed at dovilo.app.

Who It's For

Developers, indie hackers, and solo founders who want a task manager that connects to their AI coding tools and rewards focused work with something more tangible than XP. Also a strong pick for anyone who wants a Pomodoro timer and ambient sound in the same app as their to-do list.

2. Forest: Best for Distraction-Free Focus Sessions

Forest is the most downloaded focus app in this category. The mechanic is simple: plant a virtual tree when you start a session, and it grows as long as you stay off your phone. Leave the app and the tree dies.

The forest you build over time is visually satisfying, and ambient sound is included in the free tier. It's genuinely effective for building phone-off focus habits.

The limitations are real, though. Forest has no task management — you'll need a separate to-do app, which means context-switching every time you want to know what to work on next. The reward system is passive; your forest grows on its own, but you can't construct or customize it. There's no spendable economy.

Forest works well as a focus companion, but it's not a Habitica replacement in any meaningful sense. It solves a different problem.

Who It's For

Users whose main issue is phone distraction during work, and who already have a task management system they're happy with.

3. BeeDone: Best for ADHD and Apple Users

BeeDone is built specifically for neurodivergent users, particularly those with ADHD. Its standout feature is Task Roulette, which randomly selects a task when decision fatigue kicks in. AI coaching helps with task framing and prioritization.

The reward system uses XP, gems, and badges — abstract rather than visual, which works for some users but may feel thin compared to a city you can actually see growing.

Who It's For

iPhone and iPad users who struggle with task initiation and want AI-assisted prioritization. Not a strong fit for cross-platform workflows.

MainQuest offers deep RPG-style progression — character leveling, quests, a built-in focus timer — all at no cost. If Habitica's RPG loop is what you love and you just want more of it without paying, this is worth a look.

The trade-off is complexity. The system can feel overwhelming for users who just want to get things done without managing a character build. There's no city or world-building element, so visual progress is tied to character stats rather than something you construct.

It's a strong free option for users genuinely invested in RPG mechanics, but it's not designed for the developer or productivity-first audience.

Users who want Habitica-style RPG progression with a built-in focus timer and no subscription cost.

Finch uses a virtual pet bird as its central mechanic. Complete goals and self-care tasks to help your Finch grow and go on journeys. The focus is explicitly on emotional wellbeing and self-compassion rather than output or productivity.

Who It's For

Users who want a wellness companion with light goal-tracking — not a task manager or focus timer replacement.

6. Todoist: Best Pure Task Manager

Todoist is the most capable task manager on this list, with 50 million users and a feature set that covers everything from simple to-do lists to complex project management with filters, labels, and integrations.

What it doesn't have is any gamification. No reward loop, no focus timer, no ambient sound, no visual progress system. It's a clean, powerful organizer for people who find gamification distracting rather than motivating.

If you're leaving Habitica because the RPG layer feels like noise and you just want a reliable task manager, Todoist is the obvious choice. If you're leaving because you want more reward and engagement — not less — it's the wrong direction.

Users who want serious task management without any gamification layer.

No other gamified productivity app offers this.

Forest's timer is phone-lock focused. MainQuest includes a basic focus timer alongside its RPG system.

Can I use more than one of these apps together? Yes, and some combinations make sense. Forest pairs well with Todoist if you want phone-off focus sessions alongside a serious task manager. If you want task management, focus sessions, and a reward loop in a single place, Dovilo is the only option on this list that covers all three.

The gamified productivity space has more depth than it did a few years ago. Cursor AI tools have become a core part of how independent developers and solo founders actually ship software in 2026. What started as an AI-assisted code editor has grown into a broader workflow ecosystem, and the developers getting the most out of it have built deliberate daily habits around it rather than just using it reactively. This article covers how those workflows look in practice, where Cursor fits alongside other AI agents, and how to structure your day so the tools work for you instead of the other way around.

What Cursor AI Actually Does in a Developer's Day

Cursor is an AI-native code editor built on VS Code that brings model-assisted editing, multi-file context, and agentic task execution directly into your coding environment. In 2026, the most-used features fall into a few distinct categories.

Tab completion and inline edits are the baseline. Cursor predicts your next edit across multiple lines, not just the current token. Most developers leave this on by default and stop noticing it after a week, which is exactly the point.

Chat with codebase context lets you ask questions about your own repo without copying and pasting files. You can ask why a function behaves a certain way, request a refactor, or ask for a test case, and the model pulls in the relevant files automatically.

Cursor Agent (Composer in agent mode) is where the real workflow shift happens. The agent can read files, write code, run terminal commands, and iterate on errors without you stepping in at every turn. This is the feature that changed how many solo developers think about task batching.

How Solo Developers Structure Their Day Around Cursor

Developers who get consistent output from Cursor share a few workflow patterns. They are not just using AI to write code faster. They are using it to stay in a focused state longer.

Morning: Task Scoping Before You Open the Editor

The most common mistake is opening Cursor first thing and asking it to "help with" something vague. Developers who ship consistently start with a written task list before they touch the editor. They define what they want the agent to do, break it into specific units, and hand those units off.

This is where task management becomes part of the Cursor workflow rather than separate from it. A developer might have five tasks queued for the morning, each scoped tightly enough that Cursor Agent can execute one without constant guidance.

Midday: Running Agent Sessions in Parallel

By midday, many developers are running Cursor Agent on one task while handling code review, documentation, or planning for the next session. The agent works through a defined scope, surfaces errors, and proposes fixes. The developer checks in, approves or redirects, and moves on.

This parallel approach only works when tasks are well-defined upfront. Vague tasks produce vague output, and you end up spending more time correcting the agent than you would have spent writing the code yourself.

Afternoon: Review, Commit, and Reflect

Most developers using Cursor effectively treat the afternoon as review time. They go through what the agent produced, test it, commit what works, and log what needs rework. This is also when they update their task list for the next day, closing the loop on the whole workflow.

The Context-Switching Problem Cursor Doesn't Solve

Cursor handles a lot, but it does not manage your tasks. It does not know what you planned to ship this week, what is overdue, or what you promised a user in a GitHub issue. That gap is where developers lose time.

The typical setup in 2026 is a developer with Cursor open in one window and some combination of Notion, Linear, or a plain to-do app in another. Every time you need to check what you are supposed to be working on, you switch context. Every switch has a cost.

This is the problem that motivated Dovilo's MCP server integration. Dovilo Desktop runs a local Model Context Protocol server that creates a dedicated AI task queue, separate from your personal task list. Cursor, along with Claude Code, Windsurf, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI, can pick up tasks from that queue, execute them, and report back. The agent knows what it is supposed to do without you manually briefing it each session. Desktop, and with it the MCP server, is part of Pro — $2.49/month, $19.99/year or $49.99 lifetime, with a 7-day trial you start in the mobile app.

That separation matters: the AI task queue stays distinct from your personal list, so your own priorities stay clean while agents work through their assigned items.

Cursor AI Tools and the MCP Ecosystem

The Model Context Protocol has become the connective tissue between AI agents and external tools in 2026. Cursor supports MCP, which means it can connect to servers that expose structured data and actions, not just code.

For developers, this opens up integrations that were previously manual. A task manager with an MCP server can feed Cursor Agent a queue of work. A documentation tool can expose its content so the agent can reference it during code generation. A project tracker can receive status updates when a task is complete.

The practical result is that Cursor stops being just an editor and starts functioning as an execution layer for a broader system. Developers building these setups spend less time on coordination and more time on work that actually requires their judgment.

What Makes a Good MCP Integration for Developers

Not every MCP integration is worth using. The ones that stick share a few qualities:

  • Clear task definitions. The agent needs to know what done looks like. Vague tasks produce rework.
  • Separation of concerns. The AI queue should not mix with personal tasks or it becomes noise.
  • Feedback loops. The agent should report back on what it completed or where it got stuck.
  • Minimal setup. If the integration requires significant configuration every session, developers stop using it.

Dovilo's MCP server runs locally on desktop, which keeps data on your machine and avoids the latency of cloud-based integrations.

Focus and Flow: The Underrated Part of the Cursor Workflow

Cursor can generate code faster than most developers can type it. But speed is not the bottleneck for most solo developers. Sustained attention is.

The developers who ship consistently are not the ones with the fastest AI tools. They are the ones who protect their focus sessions. That means structured time blocks, minimal interruptions, and some kind of signal that the session is active and intentional.

Pomodoro-style timers have been part of developer workflows for years, but they work better when integrated with your task list rather than running in a separate app. When your timer, your tasks, and your sense of progress are all in the same place, you spend less mental energy on coordination.

Dovilo combines a Pomodoro timer with task management and adds a city-building game on top. Completing tasks earns bricks, which you spend to grow a persistent isometric city. It sounds like a small thing, but visible progress is a real motivator when you are working alone without a team to validate your output. The city grows because you shipped. That feedback loop is concrete in a way that a check mark is not.

During focus sessions, five full-screen ambient scenes — Rainy City, Midnight, Dusk, Snow, and Fog — play alongside a sound mixer that blends up to three layers from twelve options. For developers who work better with background sound, this removes the need for a separate ambient app entirely.

Integrating Cursor Into a Repeatable Daily System

The developers who get the most from Cursor AI tools in 2026 are not using it ad hoc. They have a repeatable system.

Here is what that typically looks like:

  1. Start with a task list, not the editor. Know what you are building before you ask the agent to build it.
  2. Write tight task definitions. One outcome per task, specific enough that the agent can execute without clarification.
  3. Run focused sessions. Use a timer to protect the session. Treat it as a unit of work, not an open-ended block.
  4. Review agent output before committing. The agent is fast, not infallible. A quick review catches the ten percent that needs correction.
  5. Log what shipped. Update your task list at the end of each session to create a record of progress and inform the next day's plan.
  6. Separate personal tasks from agent tasks. Mixing them creates confusion about what you need to do versus what the agent is handling.

This system works with any task manager, but it works better when the task manager and the agent are connected. The fewer manual handoffs in the loop, the more time you spend in flow.

Where Cursor Fits in the Broader AI Agent Stack

Cursor is not the only AI coding agent developers use in 2026. Claude Code, Windsurf, and Codex CLI all have active user bases, and many developers use more than one depending on the task.

The choice between them often comes down to context window size, model quality on specific tasks, and how well they fit into the rest of the workflow. Cursor's strength is its editor integration and multi-file context handling. Claude Code handles longer reasoning chains and complex refactors well. Windsurf has strong autonomous execution for well-defined tasks.

For developers running multiple agents, the coordination problem gets more complex. Which agent is working on what? What is the current state of each task? This is where a shared task queue becomes genuinely useful rather than just convenient. When all agents pull from the same structured queue and report back to the same place, you have visibility across your entire AI-assisted workflow.

Dovilo's MCP integration is built for exactly this setup. Any MCP-compatible agent can connect to the queue, so you are not locked into a single agent or a single workflow.

Building the Habit, Not Just the Setup

The biggest risk with Cursor AI tools is treating them as a configuration project rather than a practice. Developers spend a weekend setting up integrations, prompt templates, and task systems, then revert to old habits by Tuesday.

The setups that stick are the ones with the least friction. A task list you actually check. A timer you actually start. An agent queue that actually reflects what needs to get done. The technology is mature enough in 2026 that the bottleneck is almost always habit formation, not tooling.

Start with the smallest version of the system that works. One task queue. One focus session per morning. One review at the end of the day. Add complexity only when the simple version is already running reliably.

If you want a task manager that connects directly to your AI coding agents and gives you a visual record of what you have shipped, Dovilo is worth a look. It handles the task-to-agent handoff through its MCP server, runs Pomodoro focus sessions natively, and turns your completed work into a city you can actually see grow.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Cursor AI tools and how do developers use them daily? Cursor AI tools include an AI-native code editor with tab completion, codebase chat, and an agentic mode (Composer) that can read files, write code, and run terminal commands. Developers use them daily by scoping tasks before opening the editor, running agent sessions on defined work, and reviewing output before committing.

How does Cursor Agent work with task management? Cursor Agent can connect to external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). When a task manager exposes an MCP server, Cursor Agent can pull tasks from a queue, execute them, and report back, removing the need to manually brief the agent each session.

What is the MCP server and why does it matter for Cursor users? MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard that lets AI agents connect to external data sources and tools. For Cursor users, an MCP-compatible task manager means the agent can pick up structured tasks directly rather than relying on manual copy-paste or prompt engineering each time.

How do developers avoid context-switching when using Cursor? The most effective approach is keeping tasks, timers, and agent queues in one place rather than spread across multiple apps. Switching between a task manager, a timer, and the editor interrupts focus. Integrated tools that connect to Cursor through MCP reduce those interruptions.

Does Cursor work with other AI coding agents like Claude Code or Windsurf? Yes. Many developers use Cursor alongside Claude Code, Windsurf, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI depending on the task. When all agents connect to a shared MCP task queue, you can coordinate work across multiple agents without losing track of what each one is handling.

What is a good daily workflow for developers using Cursor AI tools in 2026? A repeatable daily workflow includes writing specific tasks before opening the editor, running timed focus sessions while the agent works, reviewing and committing agent output, and updating the task list at the end of each session. Keeping personal tasks separate from the AI agent queue helps both stay clean.

How does gamification help developers who use AI coding tools? Working alone without a team means fewer external signals that you are making progress. Gamified productivity tools that turn completed tasks into visible rewards — like a growing city skyline — provide that feedback loop internally. For developers using Cursor and other AI agents, where the agent handles some of the execution, tracking what you directed and shipped keeps the sense of ownership clear.

You set a per-project scope and brief so agents only see what you explicitly allow. Your mobile view shows agent notes, token usage, and cost per task in real time.

For developers who already run AI agents daily, this is a fundamentally different value proposition than anything Habitica or BeeDone offers. Your task list becomes the control surface for your AI workflow, not just a reminder system.

Pro also includes cloud sync across devices, all buildings and decorations, advanced statistics, custom themes, and priority support. The yearly plan saves 33% over monthly, and there's a lifetime option for users who prefer a one-time payment.

Where Dovilo could improve

The app is relatively new, so the city-builder content library will grow over time. Users who want deep social features or party-based accountability (Habitica's strength) won't find that here yet.

Verdict: The most complete gamified productivity app in 2026 for users who want a beautiful persistent world and, for developers, a task system that connects directly to their AI toolchain.

2. Habitica — Best for Deep RPG Gamification

Best for: Users who want the deepest gamification system and community accountability.

Platforms: iOS, Android, Web

Pricing: Free; optional subscription from $4.99/month or $47.99/year

Habitica has been in this category longer than almost anyone, and it shows. Your tasks, habits, and dailies all feed into an RPG character that gains levels, collects gear, and joins parties with other users. The social layer is genuinely strong — guilds, party quests, and accountability groups give Habitica a community feel that most competitors haven't matched.

The gamification is deep. There are pets, mounts, seasonal events, and enough progression layers to stay interesting for years. For ADHD users who need external motivation structures, Habitica's system is well-documented and widely recommended.

The tradeoffs are real, though. The visual style is retro pixel art, which won't appeal to everyone. The focus timer isn't a core feature. There's no persistent world you're building — the reward is character progression and loot, not a growing environment. And there's no MCP or agent-execution layer for developers.

Verdict: The strongest choice if community accountability and deep RPG mechanics are your priority. Less suitable if you want modern aesthetics, a focus-first workflow, or AI agent integration.

3. BeeDone — Best for AI Coaching on Mobile

Best for: Mobile-first users who want AI-powered motivation alongside gamified tasks.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free to start; in-app purchases (specific pricing not clearly public)

BeeDone takes a modern approach to gamified productivity, combining task management, XP systems, deep-work timers, and AI coaching in a mobile-first package. It's explicitly designed for procrastination and decision paralysis, and the AI coaching layer adds a dimension that pure gamification apps lack.

The app targets ADHD and neurodivergent users well, with features designed to reduce friction at the moment you're most likely to avoid starting. The visual design is cleaner than Habitica's.

Where BeeDone falls short is in the depth of its world. The reward system feels like an overlay on a to-do app rather than a persistent environment you're genuinely building. Pricing transparency is also weaker than it should be — it's hard to know what you're paying before you're inside the app. There's no city-builder metaphor and no MCP integration for developers.

Verdict: A solid option for mobile-focused users who want AI coaching woven into their gamified workflow. Less compelling for those who want a distinctive visual world or desktop agent connectivity.

4. Forest — Best Single-Focus Timer App

Best for: Users who want a simple, proven focus mechanic with real-world impact.

Platforms: iOS, Android, Chrome extension

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Forest is one of the most recognized apps in the focus-timer space, and for good reason. You plant a virtual tree when you start a focus session; if you leave the app, the tree dies. Finish the session and your forest grows. The app also partners with Trees for the Future to plant real trees, which adds genuine meaning to the mechanic.

The simplicity is both Forest's strength and its ceiling. It does one thing extremely well and doesn't try to do much else. There's no full task management system, no persistent world beyond your growing forest, and no AI layer. If you want a focus timer with light gamification and a clear conscience about your screen time, Forest is excellent. If you want a complete productivity system with deeper rewards, you'll outgrow it.

Verdict: The best standalone focus timer with gamification. Not a full productivity system, but a benchmark for how simple mechanics can create genuine daily habits.

5. MainQuest — Best for Quest-Framed Task Management

Best for: Users who strongly dislike traditional to-do lists and respond better to game framing.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free to start; specific pricing not public

MainQuest reframes your entire task list as a quest log. Tasks become missions, you earn XP, your character grows, and the whole experience is designed to make productivity feel less like a chore. The messaging is clear and the anti-checklist positioning resonates with users who've bounced off every standard productivity app.

The app is more character-centric than world-building-centric, which makes it feel closer to Habitica than to Dovilo. There's less evidence of deep focus-timer functionality or an AI integration layer. Pricing opacity is a real friction point for anyone trying to evaluate value before committing.

Verdict: A good fit for users who need game framing to engage with their tasks at all. Less suitable for users who want a full ecosystem or developer workflow integration.

6. Focus Plant — Best for Collectible Focus Rewards

Best for: Users who want a focus timer tied to a growing virtual garden with collectible elements.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Focus Plant sits closer to Dovilo's reward loop than Forest does, because it converts focus time into resources that grow a virtual environment. You collect plants, manage a garden, and the app includes distraction-blocking features to keep you on task.

The scope is narrower than it looks, though. Focus Plant is primarily a focus timer and plant collection game rather than a full task management system. There's no integrated to-do layer, no desktop app, and no AI connectivity. If you want a visually satisfying focus reward that goes slightly deeper than Forest, Focus Plant delivers. If you want task orchestration alongside the rewards, you'll need something else.

Verdict: A pleasant middle ground between Forest's simplicity and a full gamified productivity suite. Best as a focus companion rather than a primary task system.

7. LifeAt — Best for Ambient Workspace Aesthetics

Best for: Users who want a beautiful digital workspace environment with light planning tools.

Platforms: Web

Pricing: Free tier; Pro at $8/month billed yearly or $12/month billed monthly

LifeAt creates ambient virtual spaces — think cozy rooms, cafes, or nature scenes — that you work inside. It includes a planner, calendar, and focus timer, all wrapped in a visually appealing environment. The mood it creates is genuinely pleasant.

The distinction worth making: LifeAt is about workspace aesthetics rather than a reward economy. You're not earning anything or building anything based on your output. The environment is static and decorative rather than dynamic and responsive to your work. That makes it more of a focus environment than a gamified productivity app in the traditional sense.

Verdict: Strong for users who want their workspace to feel nicer. Not the right choice if you want your environment to respond to and reward your actual output.

8. Amazing Marvin — Best for Customizable Workflow Depth

Best for: Productivity enthusiasts and ADHD users who need extreme workflow flexibility.

Platforms: Web, iOS, Android, Desktop

Pricing: $8/month billed yearly ($96/year)

Amazing Marvin is one of the most customizable task managers available. It supports dozens of anti-procrastination strategies, flexible scheduling systems, and deep workflow configuration that most apps don't come close to matching. For users who've tried every productivity system and found them all too rigid, Marvin is often the answer.

The gamification angle is thin, though. There are some reward elements, but the experience is fundamentally functional rather than playful. There's no persistent visual world, no meaningful game loop, and the interface prioritizes power over delight. If you're here because you want gamification, Marvin probably isn't your app.

Verdict: Exceptional for workflow depth and customization. Not a gamified productivity app in any meaningful sense — it's a serious planning tool.

9. Finch — Best for Gentle, Emotional Gamification

Best for: Users who want a low-pressure, wellness-oriented progression system.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Finch is a self-care pet app where a small bird grows as you complete habits and check-ins. The emotional tone is deliberately gentle and guilt-free, which makes it approachable for users who find harder gamification systems stressful. It has strong mainstream appeal and genuinely positive user sentiment.

The tradeoff is scope. Finch is oriented toward mental wellness and self-care rather than task execution or work productivity. There's no focus timer depth, no desktop app, and no developer workflow integration. It proves that emotionally resonant gamification works — but it's solving a different problem than most users searching for productivity apps need solved.

Verdict: Excellent for its intended use case of gentle habit-building and self-care. Not the right tool if you need a serious work productivity system.

How the Apps Compare at a Glance

App Task Management Focus Timer Visual World AI/MCP Free Tier
Dovilo Full Pomodoro City builder Yes (Pro) Yes
Habitica Full Basic RPG character No Yes
BeeDone Full Deep work Overlays AI coaching Yes
Forest None Core feature Forest No Yes
MainQuest Full Limited Character No Yes
Focus Plant None Core feature Garden No Yes
LifeAt Light Basic Static spaces No Yes
Amazing Marvin Full Basic None No No
Finch Habits only None Pet No Yes

Which Gamified Productivity App Should You Choose?

The right app depends on what's actually blocking you.

If you want the most complete combination of task management, focus sessions, visual world-building, and AI agent integration in one app, Dovilo is the standout choice in 2026. It's the only app that connects your task list directly to AI coding agents while also giving you a persistent city that grows from your real work output.

If community accountability and deep RPG mechanics matter most, Habitica is the proven option. If you just need a clean focus timer with a satisfying mechanic, Forest still delivers. And if you're an ADHD user who wants AI coaching on mobile, BeeDone is worth trying.

Most of these apps have free tiers, so the practical advice is to try the one that fits your primary use case and see whether the reward loop keeps you coming back after the first week. That's the real test of any gamification system.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a gamified productivity app? A gamified productivity app uses game mechanics — points, rewards, visual progression, unlockables, or narrative framing — to make completing tasks and maintaining focus more motivating. The goal is to create an intrinsic reward loop that keeps you returning to your work system consistently.

Is Dovilo free to use? Yes. Dovilo has a free tier that includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, basic city building, dark and light themes, and no ads. Pro plans add cloud sync, the desktop app, MCP/AI agent integration, all buildings and decorations, advanced statistics, and custom themes.

What is the best Habitica alternative in 2026? Dovilo is the strongest Habitica alternative for users who want a modern visual world rather than a retro RPG aesthetic, or for developers who want their task list connected to AI agents. BeeDone is a good alternative for mobile-first users who want AI coaching. MainQuest works well for users who want quest framing over RPG mechanics.

What does MCP mean in a productivity app? MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI agents communicate with external tools and services. In Dovilo's case, the built-in MCP server on the desktop app allows AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI to read and execute tasks step-by-step, with the user monitoring progress from their phone.

Can gamified productivity apps help with ADHD? Many users with ADHD report that gamified apps help significantly with task initiation and follow-through, because the reward loop provides immediate feedback that plain to-do lists don't. Habitica, BeeDone, and Dovilo are all commonly recommended in ADHD productivity communities for different reasons.

Is Forest still worth using in 2026? Forest remains excellent as a standalone focus timer with a satisfying mechanic and a real-world impact through tree planting. It's not a full task management system, so users who need more than a focus timer will likely want to pair it with another app or switch to something like Dovilo that includes both.

Which gamified productivity app is best for developers? Dovilo is the only app in this category with a built-in MCP server that connects AI coding agents directly to your task list. If you use Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or similar tools daily, Dovilo's Pro tier gives you task oversight and agent execution in one place — something no other gamified productivity app currently offers.

The gamified productivity space in 2026 has real options at every level of complexity. Start with the app that matches where you are right now, not where you think you should be. A city that grows from your actual work is more motivating than a perfect system you never open.

item.title: Todoist Alternative: 7 Apps Worth Switching To in 2026
item.description: Find the best Todoist alternative in 2026 — from gamified apps to AI-native tools — with honest notes on who each one suits best.

Todoist is a genuinely solid task manager. Clean interface, reliable sync, good keyboard shortcuts. But if you've been using it for a while and something still feels off — no motivation, no focus support, no real reason to open the app — you're not alone. Most people searching for a Todoist alternative in 2026 want one of three things: more gamification, better focus tools, or something that actually connects to their AI coding workflow.

This list covers seven apps worth a real look, with honest notes on who each one suits best.

What Makes a Good Todoist Alternative?

It depends entirely on why you're leaving.

Todoist's strengths are natural language input, project hierarchy, and cross-platform reliability. Its weakness, for a lot of users, is motivational: there's no intrinsic reward for finishing tasks beyond the satisfaction of checking a box. If you're a student, a developer, or anyone who needs external feedback loops to stay consistent, that gap matters more than it sounds.

A strong alternative should cover the basics — due dates, priorities, recurring tasks — and add something Todoist doesn't. Every app below brings a distinct angle.

7 Todoist Alternatives Worth Switching To in 2026

1. Dovilo

Best for: Gamified productivity seekers and AI-native developers who want task management, focus timers, and a visual reward system in one place.

Dovilo takes a different approach to the whole idea of a to-do list. The core loop is simple: complete tasks and focus sessions, earn bricks, spend bricks to grow an isometric city. Every item you finish translates into something visible — a new building, a park, a landmark added to your virtual city.

The task layer covers everything you'd expect: due dates, priorities, categories, and recurring tasks. The Pomodoro-style focus timer awards bricks per session, so focused work and task completion both feed the same reward system. On mobile, it runs on iOS and Android. On desktop (Windows and macOS), the Pro plan adds a built-in MCP server.

That MCP server is what makes Dovilo genuinely different for developers. It lets AI coding agents — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cursor CLI, Windsurf, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI — pick up tasks from your list, execute them step by step, and report back. Each project can be scoped with a brief so agents only see what you've explicitly permitted. A mobile telemetry view shows agent notes, token usage, and cost per task, so you can monitor what's running without being at your desk.

Storage is offline-first, so the app works without a network connection. Cloud sync is a Pro feature.

Pricing: The free tier includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, and basic city building with no ads. Pro Yearly is $19.99 per year ($1.67 per month), Pro Monthly is $2.49 per month, and Pro Lifetime is a one-time $49.99 payment. A 7-day free Pro trial is available with no charge if cancelled before it ends.

Where it falls short: The city builder is a reward and visualization layer, not a standalone game. If you want deep RPG mechanics or a large social community, Habitica has more of that. The MCP and AI agent features are Pro and desktop-only.

2. Habitica

Best for: People who want RPG-style gamification with an established community.

Habitica turns your task list into a role-playing game. You build a character, earn gear, join parties with other users, and fight monsters by completing habits and dailies. The community is large and active, and the accountability mechanics — where your party members take damage if you miss a daily — are genuinely effective for some people.

The visual style is retro pixel art, which either feels charming or dated depending on your taste. There's no meaningful focus timer, and no MCP or agent-execution layer. If you're a developer looking for workflow integration, Habitica won't help there.

Where it fits: Students or anyone who responds well to social accountability and RPG progression.

3. TickTick

Best for: Users who want a Todoist-like experience with a built-in Pomodoro timer.

TickTick is probably the closest direct replacement for Todoist on this list. Natural language input, project folders, tags, priority levels, calendar view — it's all there. The built-in Pomodoro timer is a meaningful addition that Todoist doesn't offer natively.

The free tier is more limited than Todoist's, and the Premium plan runs around $35.99 per year. The interface is clean and the mobile apps are well-made. There's no gamification layer and no AI agent integration.

Where it fits: Power users who want Todoist's feature set plus a focus timer, without significantly changing their workflow.

4. Amazing Marvin

Best for: People with ADHD or complex productivity systems who want deep customization.

Amazing Marvin is built around the idea that no single productivity system works for everyone. You can configure it to behave like GTD, time-blocking, the Ivy Lee method, or a hybrid of all three. The customization depth is genuinely impressive — gamification elements exist, but as optional modules rather than a core identity.

There's no visual reward system and no focus timer built in by default. It's a tool for people who want to engineer their own system rather than adopt someone else's.

Where it fits: Productivity enthusiasts, especially those who've tried multiple systems and want something they can shape precisely.

5. Forest

Best for: People who primarily want a focus timer with a visual reward and a real-world mission.

Forest is a focus timer first. You plant a virtual tree when you start a session; it dies if you leave the app. The app also partners with a tree-planting organization, so your focus sessions contribute to real reforestation.

It's not a task manager. No to-do list, no project management, no AI integration. But if your main complaint about Todoist is that it doesn't support focused work sessions, Forest handles that one thing very well.

Where it fits: Anyone who wants a clean, mission-driven focus timer and doesn't need task management in the same app.

6. Sunsama

Best for: Professionals who want a structured daily planning ritual with calendar integration and AI features.

Sunsama sits at the opposite end of the motivation spectrum from gamified apps. It's calm, structured, and intentional. The daily planning ritual pulls tasks from integrations — Asana, Linear, GitHub, and others — and you schedule them into time blocks for the day. The Pro plan includes AI features and MCP support, which is worth noting for developers who want a planning-first workflow.

At $20 per month billed yearly, it's one of the more expensive options here. The audience is professionals who want a thoughtful planning process, not a reward system.

Where it fits: People who want structured daily planning with deep calendar and project tool integration, and who have no interest in gamification.

7. BeeDone

Best for: Mobile-first users who want gamified tasks with AI coaching.

BeeDone combines task management with XP, levels, and AI coaching in a mobile-first interface. It's lighter than Habitica in terms of RPG depth but more approachable. There's no persistent world metaphor — you level up a character rather than build something — and pricing isn't publicly listed.

The AI coaching angle is interesting if you want suggestions on how to approach your tasks, though the depth of that feature varies.

Where it fits: Users who want a mobile-first gamified experience with some AI guidance and don't need desktop or agent integration.

How to Choose Between These Apps

The right pick depends on what's actually missing from your Todoist setup.

If you want motivation through visible rewards: Dovilo and Habitica are the strongest options. Dovilo gives you a city to build toward; Habitica gives you a character to develop and a community to stay accountable with.

If you want a near-direct Todoist replacement with more features: TickTick is the easiest transition. The learning curve is minimal and the feature overlap is high.

If you're a developer using AI coding agents: Dovilo is the only app on this list that connects task management to agent execution via MCP. Scoped project briefs, step-by-step agent execution, and mobile telemetry for token usage and cost — that workflow doesn't exist anywhere else in this category.

If you want calm over motivation: Sunsama is the premium option for structured daily planning. It won't gamify your work, but it will help you plan it deliberately.

If focus sessions are your main gap: Forest handles that single job better than most. Dovilo handles it within a broader system.

A Closer Look at Dovilo for Developers

The MCP angle is worth a closer look because it's genuinely new territory for productivity apps.

When you connect Claude Code, Cursor, or another supported agent to Dovilo's desktop MCP server, the agent can see your task list within the scope you've defined, pick up a task, execute it, and mark it complete. A project brief limits what the agent can access, so your personal tasks stay separate from what you've explicitly permitted it to see.

The mobile telemetry view lets you watch this happen from your phone in real time — agent notes, token usage, and cost per task. If you're running long coding sessions and want to delegate specific subtasks to an agent while you handle others yourself, it's a workflow worth exploring.

Auto-generated JSON config snippets handle the MCP client setup, which cuts down the friction of getting started. The feature is Pro and desktop-only, but at $1.67 per month on the yearly plan — or $49.99 for lifetime access — the barrier to try it is low.

Quick Comparison

Habitica No RPG/avatar No Yes
TickTick Yes (Pomodoro) No No Limited

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free Todoist alternative? Dovilo's free tier includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, and basic city building with no ads — one of the more generous free options on this list. Habitica also has a free tier with its full RPG system. TickTick's free plan is more limited.

Which Todoist alternative is best for developers? Dovilo is the strongest option for developers who use AI coding agents. Its built-in MCP server (Pro, desktop) connects to Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and other agents, letting them execute tasks from your list with per-project scope controls and mobile telemetry.

Is there a Todoist alternative with a Pomodoro timer built in? Yes. Both Dovilo and TickTick include built-in Pomodoro-style focus timers. Dovilo ties the timer to a brick reward system that feeds the city builder; TickTick's timer is more straightforward.

What's the cheapest Todoist alternative with Pro features? Dovilo Pro Yearly works out to $1.67 per month ($19.99 per year), which is among the lowest price points for a productivity app with cloud sync, focus timer, gamification, and AI agent integration. The Pro Lifetime option at $49.99 is a one-time payment with no recurring charge.

Is Habitica better than Todoist for motivation? For users who respond to social accountability and RPG progression, Habitica's party system and avatar mechanics can be more motivating than Todoist's plain task list. The trade-off is no focus timer and a more complex interface. Dovilo offers a different gamification model — a city builder rather than an RPG — with a simpler entry point.

Can I use a Todoist alternative offline? Dovilo stores data locally by default and works without a network connection. Cloud sync is available on Pro. Most other apps on this list require a connection for sync, though some cache data locally.

Which Todoist alternative is best for ADHD? Amazing Marvin is specifically designed with ADHD users in mind, offering deep customization of task views and workflows. Dovilo's visual reward system and focus timer can also help with motivation and follow-through, which are common challenges for ADHD users. The right choice depends on whether you need customization depth or external motivation mechanics.

The Bottom Line

Todoist does a lot of things well, but "well" isn't always enough if you're not opening the app. The best alternative depends on what's actually causing the friction — lack of motivation, missing focus support, or a workflow that doesn't connect to how you work today.

If you want a to-do list that gives you something to build toward, connects to your AI coding agents, and doesn't cost much to try, Dovilo is worth downloading. The free tier is a solid starting point, and the Pro features — especially the MCP integration for developers — are priced low enough to test properly. It also offers a one-week free trial period.
